Params: One last wave gives Karenina's surfboard a gentle nudge forward.
The island stretches only a little way. A single glance takes in the edge of the high cliffs, where a colossal white mechanical tower stands against the sky.
So that's the lighthouse Larsen told me about...
A lighthouse meant to shine like a star in the heavens, yet no one remembers the last time its light touched the water.
Guided by Larsen's details, Karenina discovers the dilapidated dock tucked beneath the tower, where a handful of lifeboats rest, long abandoned.
This'll get Commandant and the others here... but...
She lifts her head and gazes up at the towering lighthouse.
In another stretch of sea, bathed in the same moonlight, the Balder sails on toward the Atlantic Eye, following its planned course.
The heavy silence aboard has lasted for some time now.
Balder, this is Karenina. Do you read me? Balder, do you read me?

According to Larsen, the lighthouse was modified to link directly with the Atlantic's undersea database. Within the waters covered by the Jormungandr node, its communications hold near-absolute priority.
The shadow of the comms blackout still lingers, and the brief wait for a reply stretches far beyond its actual seconds.
"Ksshh... ksshh... Balder reads you. Go ahead."
She gets through to the Balder.
Meanwhile, on the Balder's bridge, the operator almost bolts upright.
Our ship is down. I've secured a temporary landing position. It's unmarked on charts, designated Mirage Island. Transmitting coordinates now.
The comms erupt with a rush of urgent orders as the Balder's crew scrambles to respond, and even through the static, a current of pure joy runs beneath every voice.
Cheers and choked sobs tangle together in the transmission. For the first time since Karenina and the Gray Raven Commandant went silent, the Balder stirs back to life.
Karenina lets out a long, slow breath.
After the long dark of disconnection, after drifting and waiting without end, hope has finally spoken back to them.
Alright. Time to go get my shipwrecked friends ashore.
Northern Node Hel - Central Command Center
Northern Node Hel - Central Command Center
Sunlight spills through the cracks in the clouds. Years of snow, shaped by the wind into soft, sweeping curves, blanket the island in an unbroken stretch of white.
Two reinforcement squads from the Arctic Route Union have already reached the Hel node, and now Lucia is surveying the terrain and checking the defense systems.
The thought of her teammate has barely crossed Lucia's mind when she spots him around the corner.
Lee exchanges a few quick words with the Arctic Route Union member beside him, then catches Lucia's eye and strides over to share intelligence.
The repeaters are being replaced with Karenina's modified units. Once the fiber-optic protocol is fully deployed, I'll monitor the entire Hel from the node's control center.
While running the northern node's computation models, I also found something else... We need to reach Commandant and Karenina as soon as possible.
The island's defenses are functional, and the variety is decent, but the scale is limited.
Let's hope it all goes smoothly.
Lee and Lucia turn toward the sound. In the distance, an ARU member waves to them.
Transmission coming through! It's from the Gray Raven Commandant!
Karenina pilots the lifeboat and ferries everyone from the doomed half-ship to Mirage Island.
Using the comms station inside the island's lighthouse, you manage to establish contact with the northern node, Hel.
...So you found an island with a lighthouse and then raised the Balder.
And this island is now your temporary base?
Right. We're continuing the repeater replacement from here.
A barely audible sigh drifts through from the other end of the line.
Lucia and I have reached the Hel node. The Arctic Route Union reinforcements are already on site. Progress is steady.
Commandant, I've also picked up something else. Karenina—
Karenina's voice cuts into the comms channel.
Lee, this island we're on has a lighthouse linked to the undersea database. I pushed the new protocol through it and overwrote the compromised one.
The cables shouldn't be feeding them any more data.
Got it. I'll monitor the northern node for any anomalies.
And Karenina... there's something else, about you.
I used the northern node's computing power to verify all of the Effulgence frame's data, from its departure at Port Podesta through to the Jormungandr node.
The first leg of the voyage reads clean. But from this point—once you entered the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, inside Jormungandr's coverage—your frame began picking up a signal on a very specific frequency.
You mean that noise I've been hearing?
Strictly speaking, the frequency falls outside the detection range of current standard equipment... Hard to say if it's an actual sound wave or something else being translated into one.
Correct. My assessment is that your frame, or something in its vicinity, performed the "translation."
So... a sound only I can hear.
Karenina lowers her gaze to her hands.
She helped design this frame herself. There shouldn't be a single function in it that she doesn't know inside and out.
Karenina, what kind of sound is it?
Unlike the whale calls that accompanied Arius whenever he shows up, this "noise" doesn't seem to inflict any real damage on her frame.
Are you feeling any discomfort right now?
Karenina catches the worry in your eyes and shakes her head before she can even think about it.

...Look, we're on the clock. Those repeaters aren't going to swap themselves out. Come on, let's move! Once the mission's done, I'll go straight to Asimov and make him run every diagnostic in the book!
Karenina nudges you forward, steering you toward the shore where the rest of the team is busy with the mission.
Rarana spots you both approaching, wobbles into the air, and comes to rest on the brim of Karenina's cap.
The crew's laughter fills the air as the engine growls awake.
The lifeboat, now serving as their makeshift cable layer, pulls slowly away from the shore and glides out onto the grey-white sea.
The morning breeze brushes past them.
Rarana hooks its little mechanical claws over the side and gazes back at the fading island.
The giant white tower dwindles against the sky, and a strange sense of recognition stirs inside it, as though this scene has lived somewhere in its memory.
Her birthday fell on the very last day of the year.
By custom, this was a day for rest. People met with family they had been apart from, and they exchanged hopes for the year to come.
The data streaming across her display told the whole story.
Thousands upon thousands of well-wishes flowed overhead.
Perhaps from spending so long without sunlight, the girl's skin had grown startlingly pale, and against that sickly pallor, her already vivid hair burned even brighter.
But beneath that red drifting in the deep, the color of her soul was fading.
She hummed softly to herself, the data streaming before her flickering in and out, her substitute for candlelight.
A birthday is a milestone given meaning, the day the world welcomed you into it. And what "Happy birthday" really means is... your existence matters to me.
I'm still alive. I still exist.
The button to shut down the database sat right there within her reach. One press, and the entire transoceanic cable network would go dark.
In this world ravaged by the Punishing Virus, what catastrophe would follow if all communications were severed? Whatever it was, at least... it would prove she existed.
At least then, they would know that even in this forgotten corner of the world, she had been here.
Her fingertips brushed over the cold button, as light as a touch upon the last bloom of a spring night before it withered.
Cordelia blinked, then slowly pulled her hand back.
███ Island - Temporary Comms Station beneath the Lighthouse
2160\n███ Island - Temporary Comms Station beneath the Lighthouse
By linking the lighthouse to the undersea database, they managed to piece together a makeshift communications station on the island.
In theory, with the database's authorization behind them, their communications priority would climb dramatically.
Now they just had to wait for the full connection to the undersea database.
At last, a glimmer of hope. Cordelia breathed out her relief.
She set up her drawing board and, as she waited, watched the ocean surge over the reefs and flood the beach beyond the window.
The mechanical potted plant hovered close. The dull ache in her body had quieted, but the shiver in her soul would not stop.
The clouds are gray. The sea is gray. The damp air tastes bitter... but there's a little light on the coastline, just a sliver.
She caressed the baby's face and, as she had always done, began to describe the world to her.
Without thinking, Cordelia's brush moved across the board, painting nothing but black.
She spoke softly to the child cradled in her arms.
I just... I want to look away from this world... for a little while.
She turned her gaze back to the progress bar of the undersea database.
Cordelia cycled through the channels, her fingers working the dials. Somewhere in the static, a voice seemed to hover, faint and flickering, maddeningly just out of reach.
Cordelia!! Is that you? Can you hear me?
The taut wire inside her finally loosened, just for a second.
Kalon noticed the change in her voice. It was steadier now, and her tone had turned solemn as she spoke.
Where are you? Last time you said you'd made it to Rainbow Bridge. I heard Fenrir pulled out, so that means... Rainbow Bridge...
...The base is gone. The survivors and I are on Mirage Island, near the undersea database. Coordinates... I've sent them to you already.
What about you, Cordelia? Are you alright?
Me? I'm managing... Oh, and I have some news. Good news, the kind that matters. I found the child. She was stuck in the Atlantic with White Stork. Our people got her out.
The little one reached up and caught a strand of her red hair.
When I first saw her, she barely moved, like a little doll. But now... she cries, she yells, she kicks me in the face with her tiny feet...
And how's White Stork? I haven't been able to reach her. Wise has been worried sick.
The young woman fell silent for a moment.
...It's alright. You don't need to finish.
Kalon's voice dropped, quiet and heavy.
I'll talk to Wise. After all... she's his family...
The static over the comms thickened, growing heavier by the second.
Professor Kalon, I... I've been thinking...
I know I can't save everyone. I know I have to make my choices. But...
But why does it still feel like... I didn't do anything?
The things that mattered... why... why did they still slip away?
It was only before Kalon, the teacher who was both father and brother to her, that Cordelia could let the terror hidden inside her come spilling out.
Did you give the child a name?
Kalon spoke of something else instead.
Because of what I did, she was taken from her parents, put through experiment after experiment, and remade into something that was never supposed to have a will of her own.
And yet, whether it was our efforts or the soldiers who did their duty, she found her way to you. And she became alive, truly alive.
How many turns of fate does it take for a life that small to land safely? To grow up without breaking?
That is what makes it precious. That is why that small life deserves to be watered with the best things we have. Love. Courage. Devotion.
It is fragile, and it's so easy to break it. But what it creates, what it leaves behind, will prove its worth across all the years that follow.
Don't let it break you, Cordelia.
Cordelia drew a deep breath and managed to summon a faint smile.
I haven't given her a name yet...
Familiar faces from the base flickered through Cordelia's mind, the ones who had fallen and the ones who would never be forgotten.
She's the girl the Karenin saved.
Then name her for the ship that brought her to safety... Karenina.
Kalon's voice dropped, quiet and heavy.
Cordelia, there is something about this child. I think it's better you hear it now.
...Even with the TEC's technology stabilizing her condition, the odds of her reaching adulthood are slim. Very slim.
You know, I think someone told me something like that once... And look at me, still alive and kicking.
Compared to yours, her condition may be...
Then we do everything we can to give her a happy life, Professor Kalon. However much of it she gets.
She cut Kalon off before he could pass his sentence, lifting her face to force the swelling tears back.
The best life we can manage... whether that's long or short.
She lowered her head and began to sway her arms once more, ever so gently, humming that familiar, warm lullaby.
The mechanical potted plant glowed faintly in the stillness, quietly storing away every note deep within its memory.
Clack. The lighthouse's alarm system flickered to life.
Cordelia's brow furrowed as the report unfolded, her heart sinking with every line.
Professor Kalon, we've got a problem. The radar is showing a massive cyclone forming about a hundred nautical miles out... The projected track puts this island directly in its path.
This island's facility is barely holding together as it is... We won't survive a direct hit.
The Science Council and I will push for everything we can get.
It's just... the global situation is deteriorating fast. Every region is stretched thin.
Dispatching ships right now would not be easy. Some... political complications have even locked Port Podesta out of the equation.
How many people do you have with you?
Seventy-six... That means a heavy transport is the only viable option...
Karenina's experimental data should carry some weight.
I suppose we'll have to use it as leverage...
Static crackled in the silence between them.
Give me some time. I can make them listen.
You're due for a maintenance cycle, if I remember correctly.
You haven't missed a single checkup since the body modification surgery...
Given what this virus does, I'll just have to hope the facility that handles my maintenance is still in one piece when I get back.
She let out a small, resigned laugh.
This isn't the time for jokes like that.
Still... if you can joke, you can't be at your worst.
I'll work your maintenance into the schedule, right after the rescue. I'll be waiting for you.
The conference hall stretched out vast and cold, its stark white light spilling evenly from above and erasing every trace of shadow.
Given the urgency of the situation... this is why I have requested expedited clearance.
In my assessment, the clinical subject of the Adam experiment still warrants further observation.
With Arius confirmed dead, she may be the only remaining clinical subject through whom we can monitor the long-term trajectory of this technology.
Furthermore, on purely humanitarian grounds, we have ample justification to deploy a rescue operation.
Silence hung in the air. Then came the steady tap of a pen against the tabletop.
The report itself is clear. I have no issues with the content.
The only question is the cost in resources.
Right now, one heavy transport can pull two hundred people off an evacuation line. That is what we are losing.
And you want us to divert one into an active storm zone, to extract... seventy-five civilians and a single test subject.
The man with the scarred cheek flipped through the documents Kalon had submitted on short notice, his eyes finally coming to rest on Cordelia's file.
He skimmed it quickly, then sank into a long, heavy silence.
From the far end of the table, a pen beat against the surface in a slow, steady rhythm.
The data can wait. Their location isn't in the zone heaviest hit by the Punishing Virus. At least for now, there's no immediate threat to their lives.
According to the Science Council's meteorological data, the cyclone closest to them is intensifying rapidly.
Kalon pulled up the meteorological data on the display.
A barren island. Seventy-six people. One hundred nautical miles. We are out of time.
I want to help you, Dr. Kalon. I really do... But our transport capacity is stretched to the breaking point.
I'm not asking for a dedicated aircraft.
There should be several TEC rescue teams making their way back around now.
Even if you can't spare seventy-six seats, those planes must have some room left...
Diverting rescue teams toward a cyclone means risking their lives... And risking what few aircraft we have left, Dr. Kalon.
A note of hesitation crept into the military officer's voice.
They don't need to get close. They don't need to land.
Let the people on the island sail through the storm on their own. Once they reach calmer water on the outer edge, you airlift them from there. Is that acceptable?
The dispatcher tapped his pen and sank into thought for a long moment.
At last, he let out a sigh.
I can't guarantee how many seats will be open on those flights.
Whether they make it back or not... sigh... that's in fate's hands now.
I hope your student comes back safely. I have a daughter myself. I understand how you feel.
For the first time, a weary smile broke through the man's perpetually stern expression.
Dark clouds smothered the sky and blotted out every last trace of sunlight.
The storm had not yet taken visible shape, but the waves that relentlessly hurled themselves against the shore were already heralding its arrival.
The survivors on the island began sorting through their supplies and loading them onto the ship.
Onni, having just set down a crate, let out a breath and glanced over at Larsen, who was bent over a small notebook, scribbling intently.
Hey, you. Slacking off at a time like this?
He clapped Larsen hard on the back, and while Larsen was still startled, he snatched the little notebook straight from his hands.
What are you writing in here? Let's see... "We cannot stand against it. No, we were never meant to stand against it."
"But the moment we turn the helm, the moment we raise the sails, the moment we roar back at the sea,"
"That which could never be defied has already been defied." ...Hey, that's good! That's got weight!
L-Lieutenant Onni, please... please don't read it out loud...
Why not? Poetry's meant to be heard. Let's see what comes next...
The little commotion drew Lumi over. She slipped closer and rose onto her tiptoes, joining in on the brief moment of leisure.
"This broken wreck of a ship still thrashes on. How ugly and laughable, this last gasp of survival."
With Karenina cradled in her arms, Cordelia arched an eyebrow and made her way toward the group.
Alright... "The twilight of the end came yesterday, and it may come again tomorrow."
"Sink, then. Sink in the next moment if you must, this last ark of ours."
The words hung in the air, and a brief silence settled over everyone present.
She scraped together what little energy she had left and cracked a joke almost on reflex.
At the sight of her tired smile, Larsen buried his face in his hands, the same as ever.
The girl cut Cordelia off before she could get another word out, scrambling to salvage what little dignity Larsen had left.
I found your sketchboard while I was packing up! You left it at the lighthouse.
Cordelia lowered her gaze to the stretch of black before her.
...I can't paint anymore. Just throw it away.
Lumi glanced around, her expression uncertain.
The tall lieutenant stepped forward and propped the sketchboard open, placing it before Cordelia. Then she stood back and watched her in silence.
The waves surged over the rocks and washed across Cordelia's feet. She did not move.
He studied the deep, heavy black for a long moment, then dipped his index finger into the palette and pressed a single spot of white onto the canvas.
That's snow. Boss said... the fish taste best when it snows. Mothers love making fish soup, but the kids all want it fried.
Hot enough to warm you through, with the smell filling up the whole house.
Lyndae stared at Onni as though she had just seen a ghost.
Larsen considered for a moment, then plucked a brush from the set and carefully traced a long stroke of green across the canvas.
In the old stories, Yggdrasil is a great ash tree whose branches are home to countless living things.
At my school, there was an ash tree too. The leaves were so thick they blocked out the sun... Bright green in spring and summer, gold in autumn...
I've heard that the tropical forests are an endless sea of green, and the air smells like fruit ripening on the branch... I've never traveled that far.
Have you ever been to Akdilek?
Lumi took up a touch of golden yellow and swept a long, graceful arc across the dark canvas.
The sand burns hot under the sun. When the wind rises, the gold and orange and white grains all sing together. They move like silk. No paint ever made could match it.
That's where Sieg and I grew up.
Her eyes curved into a smile, bright and glistening. The glimmer, on closer look, was tears.
Onni nudged Lyndae with his shoulder.
She swept broad, unapologetic strokes of blue across the canvas.
Wherever I end up next, I'll always find my way back to this blue.
With Karenina cradled in her arms, Cordelia watched as that deep, dark black was slowly overtaken by patches of vivid color.
Her friends pressed in around her, offering the clumsiest, most sincere comfort they had to give.
It felt as though, once again, she wanted to see what lay beyond the horizon.
She lifted her brush and began to draw again.
(It is fragile, and it's so easy to break it. But what it creates, what it leaves behind, will prove its worth across all the years that follow.)
Mm... It's fireworks, a farewell, a well-wish, and a remembrance.
Destruction, explosions, ruin, but also beauty, blossoming, something new being born.
Cordelia took Karenina's tiny hand and dipped it softly into the paint.
A small red circle bloomed on the canvas.
Karenina, red... is the color of the sun.
When the storm passes, the sun will bring a new day.
The mechanical potted plant hovering beside her face gave off a soft glow, silently tucking every color of the world into the depths of its memory.
At last, the preparations wound down, and the survivors on the island began to board the ship one by one.
Anything left behind? Check again! We are not coming back for it!
Engineers, run every module. I want all systems confirmed operational before we cast off!
Everyone else, get to the crew mess and stay put! The ride's going to get rough! Stay where it's safe!
The shouts of those boarding, the crashing of the waves, and the howling wind all mingled together, threading a low current of anxiety through the air.
...Can this ship really survive a storm like that?
Resources here are limited. We can patch it up as much as we can... but the damage that's already done just...
Between the two of us, which one is a marine engineer?
Cordelia turned her head away, letting her gaze settle on the far-off horizon.
This is the only chance Professor Kalon could get us. There is nothing else to hope for.
That's right. I'm forcing every one of you to bet your lives on this ship.
If the worst happens... you can come find me in hell and settle the score. Though I'll probably be a few levels deeper, so you'll have to climb down.
If the bet goes bad, we've got the sea to blame.
And I'm not going to hell with any of you! When I die, I'm headed to Valhalla.
Remember to send me a message when you get down there. I want to know what a cigarette lit with hellfire tastes like.
I'm sorry, Cordelia. I wasn't trying to make things heavier...
There's a writer I like. He wrote this in his book...
"Hope is like a plant. It sprouts, it grows, and it gives you a reason to keep living."
Larsen swallowed the rest of the line—"But it can also be a wound that never heals."
Is that the writer you modeled your poem after? "This broken wreck of a ship still thrashes on..."
No! I-I mean, I wasn't trying to imply...
Alright, stop trying to fix it. "Thrashes"... it's not a bad word, actually.
Let's thrash on, then, until the very end.
In the distance, Cordelia caught sight of the towering cliffs.
Before leaving, she had taken every cornflower seed stored in the potted plant and planted them across the island's high bluffs.
There, a massive rock rose against the wind and sea, as though it could never be worn away. Into it, Cordelia carved her name.
Larsen hauled the last crate of books and supplies onto the deck and stood for a moment, watching Cordelia from a distance.
The wind caught his notebook and flipped it open to a particular page. It read:
In the dark times, will there also be singing?
In the dark times, will there also be singing?
Yes, there will also be singing.
